data.title: The origins, meaning and history of the oldest hillforts
data.excerpt: In the 10th century the traveller Ibráhím ibn Jákúb described how the Slavs laid out their forts: in watery meadows they marked out a round or square space and heaped up ramparts of earth braced with planks and stakes. This article traces where that building tradition came from — from Neolithic palisades and Early Bronze Age hillforts to the oldest Slavic hillforts of the 6th and 7th centuries.
data.metaTitle: The origins of the oldest Slavic hillforts
data.metaDescription: How and why the oldest hillforts arose: a 10th-century account of Slavic fort building and the development of defences from prehistory to the 10th century.

keyFacts.label: Topic
keyFacts.value: The origins and typological development of Slavic hillforts from prehistory to the 10th century

keyFacts.label: Key source
keyFacts.value: Ibráhím ibn Jákúb (10th century) – a description of how a lowland fortified settlement was built

keyFacts.label: The oldest Slavic hillforts
keyFacts.value: Chotomel and Zimno (the Korčak culture, the East Slavic homeland)

timeline.title: The first fortified hilltop settlements
timeline.description: The seeking out of elevated positions for fortified settlements appears as a consequence of the emerging clan-based social order – these are not yet hillforts in the true sense of the word.

timeline.title: The Únětice culture
timeline.description: Well fortified and protected settlements emerge that can already be classified as hillforts, with links to the Balkan/Minoan cultural sphere.

timeline.title: The Hallstatt–La Tène period
timeline.description: Celtic hillforts with stone walling and a palisade continue the traditions of the Final Bronze Age; later the classic Celtic oppida develop.

timeline.title: Hillforts in the East Slavic homeland
timeline.description: The oldest Slavic hillforts, Chotomel and Zimno of the Korčak cultural group, come into being; the dating of Zimno is confirmed by a find of Byzantine coins of the 6th century.

timeline.title: Pre-Great Moravian centres and the era of Samo
timeline.description: The hillforts of Tornow and Vorberg arise in Lower Lusatia, Sukow, Teterow and Behren-Lubchin among the Baltic Slavs, and in southern Moravia the foundations of Mikulčice – in the time of Prince Samo and his Wogastisburg.

timeline.title: The defeat of the Avars
timeline.description: The armies of Charlemagne defeated the Avars, which opened the way for the rise of hillfort building among the Slavs of present-day Slovakia, culminating in the era of Pribina.

timeline.title: The classic hillfort society
timeline.description: At the top of the social ladder stands a magnate or prince with his family and military retinue, as we know it from the Great Moravian milieu.

timeline.title: The testimony of Ibráhím ibn Jákúb
timeline.description: The Arab traveller describes the way the lowland type of Slavic hillfort was built – the most developed form of this building tradition.

children.text: “Most of their forts the Slavs build in the following way: they seek out meadows rich in water and thickets and mark out on them a round or square space, according to the shape and size they wish the fort to have. Then they dig all around, heaping up the earth, which they strengthen with planks and stakes. In this way they create ramparts, which they raise until the walls reach the required height. Then they measure out a gate for the fort on a suitable side and build a bridge up to it. By this they enter it.”

So much from Ibráhím ibn Jákúb, a merchant and traveller of Jewish origin from Tortosa, who visited Slavic Central Europe in the 10th century. From this valuable description of the building of a “hrad”, i.e. a hillfort, we learn about the method and the sequence of the work involved in building a Slavic hillfort. It must be borne in mind, however, that this is already a period when the building of hillforts among the Slavs had reached its most developed form and that, moreover, it concerns only one of the types of hillfort, the so-called lowland type. In order to clarify the question of Slavic hillforts we must therefore go back several centuries, to the dawn of Slavic history, and perhaps still further and deeper into the past.
Hillfort builders before the Slavs

Already in the period of the Neolithic farming cultures we encounter, in the territory of present-day Slovakia, the first hints of the building of features whose function was, among other things, collective defence. These were palisades and fences, sometimes combined with a simple rampart and ditch. This is the case, for example, among the people of the painted pottery, or among the Tisza cultural groups and the like. The seeking out of elevated positions, however, we witness only in the Eneolithic. This involved the building of fortified hilltop settlements, probably as a consequence of the emerging clan-based social order and, in general, as a consequence of changes in social relations that are difficult to specify more closely. In many places we encounter the phenomenon that it was precisely these positions that the Slavs often sought out. That does not mean, however, that we may look for any connection between them and these cultures. These are not yet hillforts in the true sense of the word, quite apart from the chronological distance between the two worlds, which were diametrically different.

A far higher level of fortifying hilltop settlements can be observed in our regions among the population which, in the Early Bronze Age, welded together the varied ethnic mixture of the Eneolithic. Here we encounter well fortified and protected settlements which can already be classified as hillforts. The advanced character of these cultures, as for example in the case of the Únětice culture, may be sought in contacts with the Balkans, that is, with the proto-Greek, or Minoan, cultural sphere. From this point in the history of the territory of present-day Slovakia, further development unfolded in the Late and Final Bronze Age. That period is already characterised by the rise of proto-Celtic entities, with the Danube region becoming the place of civilisational progress. These include, for example, the Tumulus people or the Urnfield people. It is precisely the second of these cultures that we follow under the designation Lusatian to Silesian-Platěnice in the area of Poland and northern Bohemia down to the end of the 2nd millennium BC, i.e. the arrival of the Celts. Of key importance for understanding this development was the excavation of the hillfort near Kroměříž. The hillfort was fortified from its earliest stage and presents three basic occupation layers, capturing all the important developmental changes. The youngest occupation represents an ethnic group about which the view was spread, especially in Polish archaeology, that it was a proto-Slavic element. Further research, however, resulted in a more moderate conclusion, namely that this ethnic group represents only one of the components that took part in the process of Slavic ethnogenesis. There were probably more of these components. These bold conceptions of a direct connection between the Lusatian culture and its successors on the one hand and the early Slavs on the other do nevertheless have their justification in a whole series of shared features. These include a settled, agricultural way of life, an identical burial rite, i.e. cremation burial, and not least the building of fortified settlements resembling in many respects the later early Slavic hillforts, even on identical sites. They are distinguished by a large area in elevated positions, from which we infer their primarily refuge character, for example the hillfort of Prachovské Skaly or the site of Mužský-hrada (Czech Republic). Where there are not enough elevations, in the Polish lowlands of rivers and lakes, there we find hillforts with the combined protection of rampart and water. A classic case of such a lowland water hillfort is Biskupin near Gniezno. The “Lusatian-Slavic” theory is ultimately weakened, however, by the fact that the building of a hillfort cannot reliably be regarded as an ethnic expression, even if it was closer to some ethnic groups, such as precisely the Slavs, than to others. The building of fortified settlements, the predecessors of hillforts, is encountered also in areas where we do not assume a Slavic ethnogenetic process but only later settlement, when proto-Celtic, Celtic and Germanic tribes succeeded one another.

In the period of the first half of the 1st millennium BC a further civilisational advance takes place in the Central European area. The hillforts of this period were built at considerable heights, sometimes as much as 700–800 metres. The defensive walls reached widths of several metres, strengthened with drystone walling and a palisade. The system of construction and defence of the entrance gates is already elaborate. Development proceeds in this way until the
Hallstatt–La Tène
period, i.e. the 5th–4th century BC.
Celtic hillforts

of this period are of a similar character, continuing the traditions of the Final Bronze Age. Stone and palisade remain in use; the new element is auxiliary timber structures in the building of the rampart. The hillforts still retain their high positions and thus a predominantly refuge character. From the early Celtic period we come to the era of the classic Celtic oppida, which are distinguished by a further differentiation of the hillfort’s space, i.e. the fortified centre itself with fortified baileys. Particularly complex is the system of rampart defences with lateral auxiliary abatis and protective measures preventing the enemy from gaining access to the hillfort. We distinguish several forms of lateral-type gates, tunnel-like entrances, or so-called pincer-shaped gates drawn inwards. It is precisely this last type of gate that we later encounter among the Slavs. The era of the Celtic oppida ends in our lands with the invasion of the Germanic peoples at the turn of the era.
For the
Germanic peoples

the building of hillforts is not typical. Where we occasionally encounter exceptions that confirm this rule, these mostly involve the use of captured Celtic hillforts, or the influence of the Celtic tradition. Most of the oppida conquered by the Germanic peoples, however, were plundered, demolished and subsequently abandoned.

A different situation arises only through changed social conditions. The early feudal state that was being born in territory settled predominantly by Germanic peoples needed to build administrative and power centres. This fact, together with the later threat of Viking raids, meant that the Franks, especially under the Merovingian and Carolingian dynasties, were compelled to build several classic hilltop refuge hillforts as well, alongside the already existing royal manorial courts and the so-called palatia. These were representative seats of the Frankish nobility functioning as trade, ecclesiastical and administrative centres, with court buildings, a court school and spaces for games and contests. The palatia were not fortified at all, or only lightly. The hillfort then served as a refuge for the inhabitants of the surrounding manorial courts and palatia.
The oldest Slavic hillforts

The common root of the word “gorod”, or “grad” in our territory, has an old Slavic base. Its use across the vast territory settled by the Slavs testifies that the method of defence behind the ramparts of hillforts was common to all Slavs from the earliest times. It follows from the preceding section that the Slavs were not the only ones who built hillforts. We can say, however, that they alone brought the building of the hillfort as such to perfection, that is, to the highest possible degree of functionality in terms of military defensive capability. This is also attested by the successful resistance of the hillforts of the Great Moravian Slavs against what was then the strongest military power, the Frankish Empire mentioned above. From the records of the chronicles we learn that by their massiveness and impregnability they commanded respect even from such an enemy, more advanced especially in the quality of its armament and equipment. The situation was similar in the times of Samo and his, today almost legendary, Wogastisburg (Wogastgrad).

In general, then, we may state by way of introduction that the early Slavic hillfort in its basic form draws on the traditions of the past, rooted deep in prehistory, on the traditions of the entities that took part in the process of Slavic ethnogenesis. This is also attested by the autonomous base of the terms “hrad”, “grad”, “gorod”. It is further evident that the emergence and development of early Slavic hillforts was influenced by military contact always with specific neighbouring ethnic groups. And not least it was the adoption of building traditions from the inhabitants of newly settled areas. In our case, in the Central European area, we may therefore assume the influence of the Celtic, or Roman, element.
Understandably,
the oldest Slavic hillforts
are found in the area of the so-called “homeland” of our ancestors. These are the hillfort of
Chotomel,
a marsh hillfort with a circular rampart, and
Zimno

, built on an elevation and protected by a timber palisade. They represent the realisation of the building ambitions of the early Slavic cultural group of the Korčak type, named after a find spot in the Zhytomyr region. This is a fairly distinctive Slavic group, inhabiting the territory both west and east of the
middle Dnieper

. Besides the hillforts mentioned, several hundred settlements of semi-sunken buildings belonging precisely to the Korčak type have been archaeologically investigated. The dating of Zimno is also supported by a find of Byzantine coins of the
6th century
. In a later period several further hillforts arise in this area, such as
Novotrojickoje
, which formed one of the basic centres of the later emerging
Kievan Rus

. Despite this, the occurrence of hillforts in the centre of the presumed Slavic expansion is relatively low. Here it must be borne in mind that the prerequisites for the emergence of a hillfort are certain favourable social and economic conditions, which allow a particular group of inhabitants not to take part directly in the production of agricultural goods, and also the presence of a military threat. Evidently neither of these factors was pronounced enough in the area in question to lead to the development of hillforts on any more significant scale.
The situation is already different in the
6th to 7th centuries

in Transcarpathia, in the Vistula region, that is, also in the areas where the Slavic element originated. Polish archaeology follows the early beginnings of Slavic fortification here at as many as five hillforts. Of these,
Stradów

stands out above the others by its area. It is one of the largest hillforts of Lesser Poland of all, with an area of over 20 ha, extending across a broken hillside of the Carpathians. It consists of several baileys and the centre proper. Both in its dating and in its type it best represents the character of the older hillforts of the Vistula area. Another hillfort of this area,
Chodlik

, is by contrast of the lowland type. It is formed by a triple belt of circular ramparts up to 300 m in diameter. The archaeological finds, especially finds of short spurs and spurs with hooks, suggest that the hillfort was founded sometime in the 6th century. To the period of the beginning of the 7th century we date the hillforts of
Damice and Demblín
as well as
Szczaworyź
. All five hillforts survive into the classic phase in the 10th century.

In general, for the first Slavic hillforts located in the oldest Slavic ethnogenetic area we may state their refuge character, yet already with hints of an organisation that goes beyond a purely refuge function, or beyond the form of a simple clustered fortified settlement. This holds for the oldest Transcarpathian hillforts as well as for the sites in the Dnieper region and in western Ukraine.
From the
end of the 6th century
we further know the hillforts of the Masovians and the Polans, the later
founders of the Polish state
. Archaeologically investigated were above all the hillforts of
Szeligi and Lezcyca
in the Masovian area of the middle Vistula region, as well as
Siedlemin, Daleszyn and Bonikowo

in Greater Poland. Of these, Bonikowo in particular, thanks to thorough excavation, demonstrated a gradual development from a simple smaller hillfort of 2.5 ha to a developed centre with several baileys in the classic phase of the 9th to 11th centuries. It lost its importance only with the annexation of Silesia to the Polish state, when it lost its original position as the power centre of the independent tribes of the Polans and the Silesians. After the loss of their, as we would say today, “territorial sovereignty”, it was “degraded” to the role of a frontier fortress. At this hillfort we witness a classic economic and social development, a gradual expansion and later a renewed “shrinking”, as can be observed in other areas too, everywhere where development was continuous, long-term and undisturbed by sudden changes.

Thus the hillfort in the early phase of development in the territory of present-day Poland, and not only there, most often grows up in the centre of the settled area, in the midst of the agricultural settlements it serves to protect. It is bound to its own hinterland. Among the Polans we everywhere encounter a circular fortification of relatively small extent, of a few hectares, in the midst of wetlands and marshes and between rivers. This is the case, for example, of the above-mentioned hillfort of Leczyca, whose development probably began as early as the end of the 6th century. It is a ring of fortification of oval shape measuring 140 × 80 metres, later extended by a bailey. It is a classic case of a simple palisaded rampart, an early form of early Slavic fortification which we may assume at most hillforts of the early Slavs. It is an earthen bank combined with a ditch, crowned by a simple or — as in the case of the hillfort of Leczyca — a doubled row of palisades 4 metres high, precisely such as Ibráhím ibn Jákúb describes. Of course, this hillfort too underwent further complex development down to the 12th century. And so it represents one of the classic examples of the development of the timber-and-earth rampart and of the gradual perfecting of the fortification art of the Slavs. It will therefore be discussed again later. The hillfort of Szeligi, also in the Masovian area, dated by pottery finds to the turn of the 6th and 7th centuries, was built on a natural promontory, while the part not protected by the slope was secured by a transverse rampart, which is unusual among Polish hillforts. This fact proves that an artificial circular fortification was applied only where there were no natural terrain formations suitably usable for the purposes of defence.
Further west of the areas mentioned, research dates the emergence of the oldest Slavic hillforts to the chronological horizon of the
turn of the 7th and 8th centuries

. At the same time, however, we already observe here the onset of a higher, more developed stage of social and economic life. This is attested, for example, by the thorough excavation of the hillforts of
Tornow and Vorberg

in Lower Lusatia. In this region, rich in water, use was made of sandy subsoils emerging at the surface. These were hillforts of no great extent, circular, 25 and 26 metres in diameter respectively, protected by an already structurally more complex timber-and-earth rampart. The interior of the Vorberg hillfort was almost unoccupied, with the exception of a guard structure by the gate and one elongated hut with a quern, probably a mill. The existence of shelters along the inner side of the walls was also ascertained, evidently as a temporary refuge for the needs of the defenders. By contrast, the area of the extensive unfortified bailey around the hillfort was relatively densely occupied, built up with twelve huts of larger size. Two wells, smelting furnaces and a smithy were also present. The settlement may have had around 300 inhabitants and was connected with the hillfort by a tunnel entrance. We see, then, that already in the 7th century a Slavic agricultural settlement with the presence of craft production and with hints of an extended-family community passes to a higher stage of social organisation. At its top stands the chieftain of the community, who alone resides permanently behind the ramparts of the hillfort. This tendency towards higher social organisation culminated after the settlement perished by fire in the next phase and was replaced by younger building. The change was manifested in the size of the huts and the density of occupation. The houses were smaller, able to hold only one family; the total number of inhabitants may have been around 170 persons. The hillfort too was rebuilt. In place of the shelters along the walls, classic dwellings were built. The empty centre, which originally served as a place for endangered inhabitants, was rebuilt into a manorial court consisting of several residential parts, which replaced the original simple house of the chieftain of the community. We thus see here already the germs of a higher form of social organisation, of the differentiation of social relations, i.e. hints of the formation and rising importance of a nobility. This process culminated in the 9th century, in the time of the classic Slavic hillfort society, where at the top of the social ladder stands a magnate or chieftain, or a prince, with his family and military retinue, as we know it for example from the Great Moravian milieu. But that is getting slightly ahead of events, and so back to the topic…
In the
7th century
the history of the oldest Slavic hillforts also begins to be written among the
Baltic Slavs

, in the Mecklenburg–Brandenburg region, in the lake district of the famous Lutici and Obotrites, who split into a multitude of local tribes. Reliable dating in the excavations in this area is aided by the pottery, which is typical of the Slavs here. It is distinguished by unusually bulbous forms and rich decoration.
Among the oldest here we count the hillfort near the village of
Sukow
, at the site also known as “
Alte Burg

”. It is an elevation projecting about 5 m above the marshy surroundings. At the place of the older Slavic occupation a road laid with oak trunks was discovered, which connected the hillfort with the settlement at
Klein Markow
. Again, then, a measure taken by the local Slavic inhabitants within their hillfort organisation, testifying to its advanced stage. Similarly well organised hillforts were situated at
Teterow
and at
Behren-Lubchin
. Teterow was the power centre of the
Circipani
tribe. At both hillforts a high degree of carpentry skill in the building of fortifications, roads and bridges is evident. A similar situation is also found among the tribe of the
coastal Wagri
with their centre Oldenburg, or
Starigrad
. This main hillfort of Wagria is significant also as a place of early Slavic pagan cult, of which it later became the centre.
In connection with Slavic paganism, excavation was conducted at
Faldberg
. Its task was to locate and prove archaeologically the existence of nothing less than the renowned
Rethra

itself, the centre of the cult of the god Dažbog Svarožič. Rethra as described by Thietmar of Merseburg was not found, but the presence of an early Slavic hillfort of the 7th century was ascertained. It was built on a height above a lake, with a fort and cult centre and a bailey, with three gates and dense building with houses in rows.
The situation was different
in the territory of present-day Slovakia

, where the existence of hillforts from these earliest times is not attested. This is probably a consequence of coexistence with the Avars, or rather of their domination. Even though the finds testify to an already more developed, not typically rural society, represented by the Avar-Slavic element, we cannot speak of classic hillforts here. Under the domination and influence of the Avar nomadic way of life the local Slavs evidently, so to speak, never got round to building them. This
situation changed only after
the Slavic
anti-Avar uprisings
and, not least, after the defeat inflicted on the Avars by the armies of Charlemagne at the end of the 8th century. Only after this historical turning point does the
rise of the Slavs of present-day Slovakia
begin, accompanied also by the building of hillforts,
culminating in the era of Pribina

. Development was similarly slower in the Czech lands, although here the causes must be sought elsewhere. The only exception in our area is the region of southern Moravia, probably as a result of traditional relations — commercial, craft and cultural — with the remnants of the Roman environment of the provinces of Pannonia and Noricum. The Slavs of southern Moravia, whom Avar power touched only marginally, had the opportunity to draw directly on the legacy of the building experience of the Roman centres of the Danubian Limes Romanus. That is why at
Mikulčice
we can speak
already in the 7th century

of the non-agrarian character of the settlement, fortified with a timber-and-earth rampart. Likewise the archaeological finds of craft activities at Staré Město, as well as the excavations at Pohansko near Břeclav, testify to occupation already in the pre-Great Moravian period, approximately two centuries before Mojmír’s unifying activities. Mikulčice, then, known for its luxurious equipment, jewellery and churches in the Great Moravian period, did not come into being overnight, so to speak on a green field. The foundation of this most massive centre of Moravia must be sought precisely in the 7th century, sometime
in the times of Prince Samo

. Besides the Great Moravian finds and the finds from the Avar-Slavic period of the 8th century, we also find a third, oldest horizon at this site. The Mikulčice occupation already covered an area of about 50 ha at that time; the settlement was dominated by a lightly fortified fort area with an area of 4 ha. It was built in the manner of a manorial court, surrounded by a rampart built in the manner of the classic early form of Slavic fortification. The socially already differentiated environment of non-agrarian character, with lively craft and trade production and activity, is attested among other things by numerous finds of riding spurs with hooks, typical of this period. These finds testify to a superior social stratum of individuals, or a ruling stratum supported by the forming mounted retinue of a magnate or prince, which gradually developed into the elite fighting component of Slavic hillfort society. Likewise the pottery finds are not limited to simple, undecorated, handmade vessels of the Prague type. On the contrary, the pottery products are richly decorated with multiple wavy lines of the Danubian type and also with the technique of burnished patterns. A similar fortified centre, protected by a palisade and a ditch, is encountered also at
Staré Město

. The last of the pre-Great Moravian Slavic “fortresses” we find in the form of the hillfort of Líšeň near Brno, where we again have numerous finds of riding spurs. Of course, Slavic occupation is evident from the earliest times throughout the territory of former Czechoslovakia, but we can speak of the oldest hillforts only in the few cases given above.

In conclusion to the part devoted to the oldest Slavic hillforts, we cannot fail to mention the most famous of all, namely the mythical Wogastisburg. A separate section of this blog is devoted to this site:
